title: Indian Student Applications to U.S. Colleges Drop 15% as Visa Rules Tighten
excerpt: The sharpest single-country decline in nearly a decade of Common App tracking comes amid four-year visa caps, a proposed $100,000 OPT fee, and mounting H-1B uncertainty for Indian families.
body:
• Indian undergraduate applications to U.S. colleges through Common App fell 15% in the 2025-26 cycle, dropping from roughly 16,900 to 14,424 applicants
  • The decline is the sharpest single-country drop in nearly a decade and drove an overall 10% fall in international applications — the steepest on record
  • Policy shifts including four-year visa caps, a proposed $100,000 OPT fee, and H-1B uncertainty are reshaping the cost-benefit calculation for Indian families considering U.S. education

The number of Indian students applying for first-year undergraduate admission to U.S. colleges through the Common Application fell 15 percent during the 2025-26 admissions cycle, reversing nearly a decade of rapid growth and widening the gap with China at a time when federal visa policies are raising fundamental questions about the long-term value of an American degree for international students.

India recorded 14,424 applicants, down from approximately 16,900 in the previous cycle, according to Common App's end-of-season report released on August 20. The decline was sharper than the 2 percent fall recorded for China, which retained its position as the largest source of international applicants with 18,435 students. The gap between the two countries now stands at 4,011 — after narrowing to roughly 1,000 during the 2023-24 cycle when India appeared poised to overtake China.

Part of a Broader International Retreat

The drop from India drove a broader contraction. International applicants overall fell 10 percent from the previous year — the steepest decline recorded by Common App since the organization began standardized tracking. Applicants from Asia, the largest non-U.S. source region, declined 11 percent to 79,287. Applications from Africa fell 17 percent, with Nigeria down 21 percent and Ghana declining 34 percent.

The contraction stands in sharp contrast to domestic trends. A total of 1,527,328 first-year applicants used Common App during the cycle, up 2 percent. Total applications rose 6 percent, with each applicant submitting an average of 7.06 applications, up from 6.79 the previous year.

Common App did not identify a specific reason for the decline in Indian applications.

Policy Shifts Reshaping the Calculation

Higher education researchers attribute the downturn to a series of federal policy changes that have made the U.S. a riskier destination for international students.

In July, the Department of Homeland Security finalized a rule ending the decades-old "duration of status" system, which since 1979 allowed F-1 student visa holders to remain in the U.S. for as long as they were enrolled in an accredited program. Under the new rule, student visas are capped at four years. Students in longer programs — including combined bachelor's-master's degrees and Ph.D. tracks that typically require five to seven years — must now apply for formal extensions through USCIS, facing potential mid-degree denials.

"The prospect of six-figure fees attached to post-graduate employment options, combined with strict four-year stay limits, has dramatically shifted the cost-benefit analysis for prospective families in India."

— Global Net News analysis

Compounding the visa changes, administration officials are considering a proposed $100,000 fee for foreign graduates seeking to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT), the 12-month post-graduation work program that serves as the primary stepping stone to H-1B visa sponsorship. STEM graduates currently qualify for a 24-month OPT extension.

Economic Fallout for U.S. Universities

The financial stakes are substantial. International students contributed $41.77 billion to local U.S. economies during the 2025-26 academic year through tuition, housing, and living expenses, according to Common App findings. That figure is projected to fall to $38.37 billion for 2026-27 — a net loss of $3.4 billion in a single year.

NAFSA: Association of International Educators projects that total international enrollment could drop by up to 110,000 students for Fall 2026, sliding from 1.169 million to as low as 1.057 million. Public universities that depend heavily on international tuition premiums to subsidize domestic operations would be hardest hit.

A coalition of higher education groups and unions has sued over the four-year visa cap rule, arguing the administration overstepped its authority. A group of 30 U.S. senators also wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio about a shortage of visa appointments at some embassies.

What This Means for Indian Families

For Indian families — who represent the largest international student demographic on American campuses with more than 352,000 students enrolled as of February 2026, according to SEVIS data — the policy landscape has shifted fundamentally. The combination of visa uncertainty, potential six-figure OPT fees, and an increasingly restrictive H-1B pathway is pushing families to reconsider alternatives in Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, all of which continue to market post-study work rights to international students.

India's decline followed almost a decade of expansion. Common App recorded about 7,900 first-year applicants from India in 2016-17. By contrast, U.S.-based applicants identifying as Indian grew 6 percent in the latest cycle to 40,949 — suggesting the pipeline of Indian-origin students already in the U.S. remains robust even as new arrivals pull back.
